### ⏳ Deadline, carried from triage

The entry is pending and unconsumed, so `changeset version` copies it **verbatim** into the CHANGELOG. The window closes at the next release of its package; after that, repairing it is rewriting history. ⚠️ Triage ordered this **ahead of its priority band**: ⛔ do not let a p2 label queue it behind every p1.

### ⛔ The instruction that makes this card not a number-swap

Triage was explicit: ⛔ **do not write 644 or 649 into the text.** Those are today's readings on two refs and they will rot exactly as 656 did. The repair is to make the sentence stop hard-coding a count — or, if a number must stay, to name the ref it was measured at.

⭐ The sharper half of the defect, and the reason it is not cosmetic: of the two occurrences, one merely **cites** a number and the other says **"re-measured here"**. A false reading that claims its own freshness is worse than one that cites no source, because the second invites a check and the first forecloses it. Whatever replaces it must not make that claim unless the act writing it actually measured.

<sub>Read at 2026-09-17T18:33Z.</sub>

⚠️ **Half-state recorded rather than quietly repaired.** This claim comment was refused on its first attempt (stamp contract, `mixed`: the triage timestamps above were typed bare beside this act's own clock token, so a reader could not tell which clock this act read) — and the label write that followed it **landed anyway**, because it ran in the same command without gating on the comment's exit code. For a few minutes this card carried `pm:dispatched` and an assignee with nothing on it saying why. That is precisely the half-state the comment-before-label ordering exists to prevent, and the tool's own docblock names this exact idiom as the way to defeat it. Repaired in the same shift, by the seat that caused it.
